Marriage Card Game Rules: Maal, Tiplu and Settlement

Marriage is Nepal's favourite rummy-style game, played with three decks and 21 cards each. This guide covers play, maal points and how to settle up.

Settling a hand? The Marriage point calculator works out every payment for you.

Marriage rules vary a lot between families and groups. Below are the most common rules — agree on anything you play differently before dealing.

Players and cards

Marriage is played by 2 to 5 players (some groups play with 6) using three standard 52-card decks shuffled together. Some groups add printed jokers (often called man cards). Each player is dealt 21 cards. The rest form the draw pile, and one card is turned face up to start the discard pile.

The sets

  • Sequence: three or more cards in a row of the same suit, e.g. 5♥ 6♥ 7♥.
  • Pure sequence: a sequence made without any joker.
  • Trial: three cards of the same rank in different suits, e.g. 9♠ 9♥ 9♦.
  • Tunnela: three identical cards — same rank and same suit, e.g. three K♣. A tunnela counts as a pure set.
  • Dublee: a pair of identical cards (same rank and suit).

Turns

On your turn, draw one card — from the draw pile or the top of the discard pile — then discard one card. You always hold 21 cards between turns.

Seeing the maal

Before jokers count for you, you must "see" the maal. To do that, you show three pure sets (pure sequences or tunnelas) on your turn. You then look at the hidden tiplu card (the cut joker) and can use jokers from then on.

Alternatively, a player can take the dublee route: show seven dublees to see the maal, and finish with an eighth dublee.

Tiplu and the jokers

Once the tiplu is revealed, these cards become jokers (wild cards):

  • Tiplu: same rank and suit as the cut card. With three decks there are three tiplus.
  • Poplu: one rank above the tiplu, same suit.
  • Jhiplu: one rank below the tiplu, same suit.
  • Alter: same rank and same colour as the tiplu, different suit.
  • Ordinary jokers: same rank as the tiplu in the other-colour suits. Wild, but worth no points.

Example: if the tiplu is 6♥, then 7♥ is poplu, 5♥ is jhiplu, 6♦ is alter, and 6♠ and 6♣ are ordinary jokers.

How maal points work

Maal is the points value of the jokers and special sets you hold. These values are the most common:

Card or setMaal points
Tiplu (each)3
Poplu (each)2
Jhiplu (each)2
Alter (each, if your group counts it)5
Marriage — jhiplu + tiplu + poplu together10
Tunnela shown before seeing5

Many groups give bonus values for holding two or three of the same maal card, or for a tunnela of tiplu. These house values differ widely — write yours down before the game. The calculator only needs each player's final maal total, so it works with any table of values.

Finishing a hand

A player who has seen the maal wins the hand by arranging all their cards into valid sets (jokers allowed) and making a final discard. Everyone then shows their hand and counts their maal. Only players who have seen the maal can count theirs.

How to settle at the end

  1. Add up the total maal of every player who has seen. Players who haven't seen count as zero.
  2. Each player's maal result = their maal × number of players − total maal. A positive number means they collect; negative means they pay.
  3. Losers pay the winner a fee: commonly 3 points from each player who saw the maal and 10 points from each player who did not.
  4. Dublee finish: many groups add a small bonus (often 5 points) from each player when the winner finishes with dublees.

Worked example

Four players. Asha wins with 8 maal. Bikash saw and has 3 maal. Chandra saw and has 0. Dipa never saw the maal. Total maal = 8 + 3 + 0 = 11.

PlayerMaal resultFeeNet
Asha (winner)8×4 − 11 = +21+16+37
Bikash (seen)3×4 − 11 = +1−3−2
Chandra (seen)0×4 − 11 = −11−3−14
Dipa (unseen)−11−10−21

The nets always add up to zero. Over a session, keep a running total and settle once at the end — the calculator's Settle up button shows the fewest transfers needed.

Kidnap and Murder variants

  • Kidnap: a player who hasn't seen the maal loses their joker points to the winner.
  • Murder: a player who hasn't seen the maal loses their joker points, but they don't go to the winner.

21-card vs 31-card Marriage

21-card Marriage is the standard game described on this page: three decks, 21 cards each, three pure sets to see the maal, seven sets to finish.

31-card Marriage is a longer house variant with bigger hands, so hands take more turns and more sets must be built to finish. Because its details change from group to group, agree on these before you deal: how many decks, how many pure sets are needed to see the maal, whether the dublee route is allowed and how many dublees it needs, and the maal values. Settlement works exactly the same way, so the calculator handles both versions.

Frequently asked questions

How many points is a tiplu worth in Marriage?

In the most common rules a tiplu is worth 3 maal points, and poplu and jhiplu are worth 2 each. A marriage (jhiplu, tiplu and poplu together) is worth 10.

What does it mean to see the maal?

Seeing the maal means showing three pure sets (pure sequences or tunnelas) so you can look at the tiplu card. Only players who have seen the maal can use jokers and count their maal points.

How much does an unseen player pay in Marriage?

Commonly, each player who did not see the maal pays the winner 10 points, and each player who saw pays 3. Unseen players also count zero maal.

How do you calculate Marriage points at the end of a hand?

Add up the maal of everyone who has seen. Each player's result is their maal times the number of players, minus the total maal. Then each loser pays the winner the seen or unseen fee.

What is a dublee in Marriage?

A dublee is a pair of identical cards of the same rank and suit. Seven dublees let you see the maal, and an eighth dublee finishes the game.
